title: The 1959 Havana festival trip with the Last Straws
summary: Mayor Morrison took three New Orleans bands to Havana; they played a parade and were made to black their faces.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Uh, you made a trip to Cuba just recently, Joe. Oh, yeah. Tell us about that.
Well, that was, that was a lot of fun.
Just how it started and everything. Well. Who do you saw?

Well, they, they had a, they had a festival in Cuba, which is very like Mardi Gras here, only it wasn't on Mardi Gras. It was on May the 1st, which is, and around that time, I believe the thing's been going on a month, mainly on weekends. Very like Mardi Gras here, only a little wilder. More frightening. Uh, like here, you're, if you're not with Zulu, all you got is a lot of drunk people wandering up and down with drinks in their hands. There, they were all seen to be dancing in the street, passed on, packed on mass, you know, I mean, like soldiers, tight as soldiers, very old streets of them, you know, doing the cha-cha-cha and, uh, hitting all sorts of things, you know, or everything you could hit. And, uh, they had a big parade, I think that since the revolution, they've been kind of scared that the tourist trade's falling off, you know, all the gambling casinos are empty and that. So, uh, the municipality of Havana invited, uh, representatives from, I think, every country in the hemisphere to, uh, come and have a representative of some kind of festival that, uh, those countries have, and they picked New Orleans to represent America, and Mayor Morrison went over with three bands. Ours was one of them. And, uh, uh, I used the last straws, you know, and Roy Liberto's band and, uh, uh, Hector Fontana's band. And, uh, we went over and we were supposed to portray a, uh, brass band, a Negro marching band, and, uh, they had about a dozen other people all dressed up as typical old New Orleans characters. Because, you know, it sounds corny, but it was pretty impressive for what they wanted. You know, it wasn't all like that. Uh, black, everybody had black face and somebody would have a basket of, uh, strawberries or selling firewood or something. I'm trying to remember some of the other things. Uh, and, uh, we, we all got very, uh, huffy and refused to black our faces and that, um, because we thought it would be in bad taste and so forth. But, uh, it was impressed on us that, uh, we were damn lucky to go over there by the woman that had nominated our band to represent New Orleans and so forth. So everybody swallowed their pride and black their face. My, my shirt still isn't clean yet. They told us it was washable and stuff, but it wasn't. And we, approximately, we rehearsed like mad trying to play like a New Orleans brass band, you know, wasn't quite the right lineup, but it, we, I think we did pretty well. I still, to see some photographs, they got it all televised. They got a film of it at WDSU. And, uh, they had this and a couple of floats and so forth and Vic Shiro on a horse representing somebody with a flag or something and presented the flag to the mayor of Havana. And, uh, had rather the big Rex floats and Roy La Bertana thing. And I think we did pretty well out of all the countries. We led the parade, but the, the only ones that I, I really remember seeing, things were a little confused towards the end of the parade, but the, the only ones I remember seeing after we'd got off the route, you know, the parade route with the Brazilians and they had some kind of troops that they had from, uh, their festival, they have a Mardi Gras in, uh, Brazil. Oh, they were wonderful. They had us beat. But we did pretty well. It was very interesting and everybody was very pleased about it. And this, they thought this was just it, you know. I really enjoyed it over there. They don't have much jazz over there. There's one place they've got so much of their own stuff that, you know, Yeah. You know, that, uh, more rhythmic stuff.
